contents.text: You can use these properties to tell whether a substance is a mineral, a rock, or neither.

subheader.text: Minerals and rocks are not made by organisms.

subpoints.text: Organisms make their own body parts. For example, snails and clams make their shells. Because they are made by organisms, body parts cannot be minerals or rocks.
Humans are organisms too. So, substances that humans make by hand or in factories are not minerals or rocks.

content.text: Rainwater collected in a crack in a rock and froze. The water expanded as it froze, splitting the rock into smaller pieces.

explanationText.text: In this example, the ice broke the rock into smaller pieces, forming sediment. But the ice did not move this sediment away from where it was formed. So, this is an example of weathering, not of erosion.

content.text: As a glacier moved over rock, ice at the bottom of the glacier ground the rock down into sediment. This sediment was carried away by the glacier.

explanationText.text: In this example, the glacier moved the sediment away from where it formed. So, this is an example of erosion.

content.text: Tree roots grew between small cracks in a rock. As the roots grew bigger, they broke the rock apart.

explanationText.text: In this example, the tree roots broke the rock into smaller pieces, forming sediment. But the roots did not move this sediment away from where it was formed. So, this is an example of weathering, not of erosion.

. Sedimentation often happens when loose grains settle to the bottom of a lake, sea, or river.
As sedimentation continues, new layers of sediment bury the older layers. The weight of these layers causes the loose grains of sediment to squeeze closer together. This process is called
Eventually, the compacted sediment becomes rock through a process called
. During cementation, minerals form in the tiny spaces between the grains of sediment. These minerals hold the grains together to form solid sedimentary rock.

explanationText.text: The processes that make up the rock cycle are driven by the transfer of energy. One example of an energy transfer is when the flow of heat causes rock to crystallize. Another example is when gravity causes water in a river to flow downhill and wear away rock along the riverbed. As gravity pulls water down a slope, the water's potential energy turns into kinetic energy that can be transferred to the rock along the riverbed and cause erosion.

content.text: Igneous rock forms as lava crystallizes.

explanationText.text: When lava gets cool enough, it can crystallize into igneous rock. But this does not directly depend on gravity. Crystallization is caused by the lava losing thermal energy.

content.text: Grains of sediment settle to the bottom of a lake.

explanationText.text: When sediment settles in water, the grains are being pulled toward the ground by gravity.
